issues.description: Participants are tested and analyzed as individuals, but they are recruited, exposed to misinformation, and randomized to conditions as dyads (pairs). Both members of a pair interact during the collaborative recall phase, meaning their responses are correlated. Treating 240 individuals as 240 independent observations violates the independence assumption of ANOVA, inflates effective N, and risks seriously inflating Type I error. The proper unit of analysis is the dyad (N=120), and a multilevel or dyadic analytic framework is required. This issue is compounded by assigning both members of each pair to the same condition, making pair-level clustering the primary sampling unit.
issues.quote: The sample size will be set at 240 people (120 pairs)... The results will be analyzed by means of a two-factor ANOVA, with one within-subjects factor with two levels (discussed vs. non-discussed items) and one between-subjects factor with four levels

issues.description: The Procedure section clearly states the individual memory test consists of 20 open-ended questions. The Analysis Plan then states the test 'will also use the two-alternative forced-choice format.' These are fundamentally different response formats with profoundly different implications for sensitivity, scoring, susceptibility to misinformation, and comparability with prior studies using the MORI paradigm. The inconsistency indicates that at least one description is incorrect, and the reader cannot determine which format will actually be used. This makes the study plan non-reproducible as written.
issues.quote: The test will contain 20 open-ended questions... In the present research, the individual memory test will also use the two-alternative forced-choice format.

issues.description: Section 1.1 explicitly states: 'we decided to place the methods inducing resistance to misinformation before the collaborative recall phase (that is, before exposing participants to misinformation). The main reason for that is that we wanted to inoculate participants against the influence of misinformation before it could take effect.' However, the Procedure section lists the order as: (1) watch movie, (2) collaborative recall, (3) interventions, (4) individual memory test—placing all three interventions firmly AFTER the collaborative recall. The Introduction also says 'we decided to place the warning after the collaborative recall.' These three descriptions are mutually contradictory. The entire theoretical rationale (inoculation before misinformation) depends on the timing, so this contradiction fundamentally undermines the stated theoretical justification for the design.
issues.quote: What is important, we decided to place the methods inducing resistance to misinformation before the collaborative recall phase... [vs.]... the third phase will take place: it will consist in the procedures to reduce vulnerability to misinformation

issues.description: The Extended Warning condition explicitly reveals the experimental deception to participants: it tells them that their partner actually saw a different version of the movie and explains why the deception was applied. This means participants in this condition are, in effect, debriefed before completing the individual memory test. Any reduction in memory conformity in this condition could be attributed entirely to the trivial reason that participants now know their partner saw different content—not to any theoretically interesting psychological mechanism (e.g., altered consistency assumption, increased metacognitive vigilance). This makes it impossible to interpret null vs. significant effects of Extended Warning in a theoretically meaningful way and confounds the manipulation with simple awareness of the experimental setup.
issues.quote: Extended warning, informing that the partner actually saw a different version of the movie and informing why the deception was applied... an enlightenment regarding the purpose of the deception.

issues.description: The Design section states that 'discussed and non-discussed items will be fully counterbalanced,' implying that different pairs will discuss different subsets of critical items so that each item appears in both the discussed and non-discussed conditions across the sample. However, the Procedure section states that 'each pair will discuss the same set of four critical details during the collaborative recall phase. For example, all pairs will talk about Eric's cap color and his company logo.' If every pair discusses the same four items, there is no counterbalancing. This means the discussed and non-discussed items differ intrinsically in their content, memorability, and susceptibility to misinformation, creating a permanent confound between item type and discussion status.
issues.quote: discussed and non-discussed items will be fully counterbalanced... In order to ensure sufficient discussion, each pair will discuss the same set of four critical details during the collaborative recall phase.

issues.subcategory: absence of suspicion / awareness check for MORI manipulation
issues.description: The validity of the entire MORI paradigm rests on the assumption that participants genuinely believe they are watching the same film. If either member of a pair suspects or discovers they saw different content (e.g., from noticing visual artifacts, seeing a partner's different response, or having prior knowledge of the MORI technique), the memory conformity phenomenon is fundamentally altered. The manuscript includes only a free-response question about the perceived purpose of the study. There is no systematic, validated measure for detecting awareness of the two-version manipulation, no predefined criterion for excluding pairs in which at least one member suspected the manipulation, and no analysis plan addressing how such cases would be handled.
issues.quote: the subjects will be requested to say what they think the real purpose of the study was. Their responses will be recorded for exploratory analysis of any relationship between hypothesis awareness and performance.

issues.description: The analysis plan specifies that four indices will be derived and analyzed using ANOVA: (1) correct answers, (2) misinformation-consistent answers, (3) other answers, and (4) total answers. These four indices are mathematically constrained (correct + misinformation-consistent + other = total), making them non-independent. Running separate ANOVAs on all four without a multivariate approach (e.g., MANOVA) or multiplicity correction substantially inflates the familywise Type I error rate. Furthermore, no correction strategy is specified for the follow-up pairwise comparisons between conditions, which further compounds the multiple comparisons problem.
issues.quote: We will explore the individual memory test's scores for the critical details using analysis of variance (ANOVA), using all four indices: the number of correct answers, number of answers consistent with misinformation, other answers, and the overall number of answers.

issues.description: None of the three interventions have manipulation checks. For Extended Warning, there is no measure of whether participants actually became more skeptical or updated their consistency assumption. For Education about Memory, there is no test of whether participants acquired or retained the presented memory knowledge. For Demonstration and Motivation, there is no measure of whether participants felt more vulnerable to influence or more motivated to resist it. Without manipulation checks, null results for any intervention are uninterpretable: they could reflect genuine ineffectiveness of the psychological mechanism or simply a failed manipulation.
issues.quote: The main goal of this proposal is to analyze the efficacy of three possible methods of reducing memory conformity. These are (1) Extended warning against misinformation, (2) providing detailed knowledge about the fallibility of memory (we called this method Education about memory), and (3) demonstrating the vulnerability of memory and motivating subjects to overcome it (called Demonstration and motivation).

issues.subcategory: pre-classification of discussed items as misinformation
issues.description: The analysis plan states: 'while scoring the individual memory test accuracy on the discussed questions (items containing misleading information), we will categorize all discussed items as having contained misinformation, as the collaborative recall procedure is designed to expose participants to their partner's differing version of events.' This is problematic because it assumes misinformation was delivered regardless of what actually happened during the discussion. A partner might have said 'I don't know,' given an answer consistent with the target participant's own version (e.g., via guessing), or been interrupted. Blanket classification inflates the denominator of misled trials and misrepresents actual misinformation exposure. The actual content of each discussion (which was recorded) should be used for individual-level scoring.
issues.quote: while scoring the individual memory test accuracy on the discussed questions (items containing misleading information), we will categorize all discussed items as having contained misinformation, as the collaborative recall procedure is designed to expose participants to their partner's differing version of events.

issues.description: In the Demonstration and Motivation condition, the DRM feedback explicitly mentions 'thief' as one of the critical lures ('See if you have written down any of the words: doctor, window, sweet, thief'). The MORI film depicts a thief (Eric the electrician who steals objects). Activating the concept of 'thief' through explicit mention immediately before the individual memory test about Eric could semantically prime crime-related concepts and affect recall of the film. This creates a condition-specific confound that could influence the outcome independently of the intended motivational mechanism, making it impossible to isolate the effect of the 'demonstration' component.
issues.quote: At this moment in this group, the experimenter will give the following information to the participants: 'Thank you for completing this memory task. Please take a look at your sheets now. See if you have written down any of the words: doctor, window, sweet, thief.'

issues.description: The control condition consists of a podcast about 'soft skills related to social attitudes,' which is mismatched with the experimental conditions on multiple theoretically relevant dimensions: content (unrelated to memory or cognition), cognitive demand, relevance to the task, and alertness-inducing properties. An ideal active control would be equated in duration, modality (podcast), and cognitive engagement, while differing specifically in memory-relevant content. The current control confounds the effects of any memory-relevant content with the simple act of being exposed to memory-related information, making it impossible to distinguish specific effects of the interventions from non-specific arousal or task-relevance effects.
issues.quote: In the control group, participants will listen to a podcast concerning soft skills related to social attitudes.

issues.subcategory: extreme heterogeneity in effect size estimates for power analysis
issues.description: The power analysis for detecting the memory conformity effect is based on only two studies, with effect sizes of Hedges' g = 1.92 (Ito et al., 2019) and g = 0.38 (Kękuś et al., 2020)—a five-fold difference. The manuscript acknowledges this 'rather large difference' and applies random-effects meta-analysis to obtain a joint estimate of g = 1.13. However, with only two studies and such extreme heterogeneity (I² would be very high), the pooled estimate is unreliable and its confidence interval extremely wide. The sample size conclusion ('a much larger sample was assumed, it can be stated that the power to detect the memory conformity effect will be sufficient') is insufficiently justified given this uncertainty. The Ito et al. result uses a multinational sample, and using the Polish subsample specifically would be more appropriate for this Polish-sample study.
issues.quote: The existing results as regards effect sizes are Hedges' g = 1.92, N = 55 (Ito et al., 2019) and Hedges' g = 0.38, N = 74 (Kękuś et al., 2020). Given the rather large difference in effect sizes between both studies, random effects were assumed while calculating the joint effect size, which was 1.13.

issues.description: The manuscript argues that normative influence 'is completely ruled out in this study' because participants complete the memory test individually without any interpersonal comparison. This conflates the site of normative influence with the mechanism. Normative influence can operate during the collaborative recall phase (e.g., a participant may suppress their correct memory during discussion to avoid conflict) and produce a carry-over effect on the individual memory test through social compliance becoming internalized or through source confusion. Dismissing this mechanism entirely without empirical justification weakens the theoretical framework and leads to overconfident claims about which mechanisms the interventions target.
issues.quote: we assumed that the normative impact explanation of the memory conformity effect is completely ruled out in this study: participants work on their own and do not compare their answers with anybody, therefore there is no cost of disagreeing.

issues.subcategory: uncertain and potentially inaccurate correlation estimate for power analysis
issues.description: The within-subjects correlation between discussed and non-discussed item scores is estimated as r = 0.07, based on two studies. This extremely low correlation is used in the power analysis for the mixed ANOVA. In within-subjects designs, the within-person correlation directly determines the error term and, thus, statistical power. Using a value close to zero is (conservatively) equivalent to assuming no individual differences in overall memory performance, which is implausible. However, any error in this estimate systematically biases the power calculation. The estimate from only two studies with a combined N of ~130 has very wide uncertainty bounds, and no confidence interval or sensitivity analysis for this parameter is reported.
issues.quote: The joint correlation of results in the discussed and non-discussed items in both studies available was 0.07. Under such conditions, the sample size required for 90% power was 18.

issues.description: The only prespecified exclusion criterion is 'technical problems during the experimental session.' There are no exclusion criteria for: (a) participants who indicate awareness of the two-movie manipulation; (b) participants with prior knowledge of the MORI technique or the stimulus film; (c) participants who fail to engage with the intervention (e.g., report not listening to the podcast); (d) pairs in which no disagreement occurred during collaborative recall, meaning no misinformation was actually delivered; or (e) participants with known memory disorders or who fail a basic comprehension check. These omissions could introduce substantial noise and invalidate key assumptions of the design.
issues.quote: We will exclude participants in the case of any technical problems during the experimental session.

issues.subcategory: speculative cross-domain application of inoculation theory
issues.description: The Demonstration and Motivation condition is explicitly motivated by Sagarin et al.'s (2002) inoculation-based resistance to persuasion by illegitimate authorities in commercial advertising. The theoretical leap from resistance to fake expert endorsements in ads to resistance to co-witness misinformation in memory tasks is substantial and largely unargued. The mechanisms are plausibly different: advertising resistance involves identifying and discounting a source's illegitimacy, whereas memory conformity involves source monitoring and confidence calibration about one's own recollections. The transfer is asserted rather than justified.
issues.quote: This was inspired by existing research on resisting social influence presented by Sagarin, Cialdini, Rice, & Serna (2002)... We adapted the ideas from the research described above in the hope that it may be useful in mitigating memory conformity.

issues.subcategory: limited scope of exploratory DRM analysis
issues.description: The analysis plan states that DRM results 'will be used as a possible predictor of the results on the MORI technique' as an exploratory analysis. However, the DRM task is only administered to participants in the Demonstration and Motivation group. This means the analysis is restricted to one of four groups, is based on approximately 60 participants, and cannot establish whether individual differences in DRM susceptibility predict MORI susceptibility in general or only in the context of the DRM demonstration. This important limitation is not acknowledged, and the analysis plan is vague about what statistical model will be used.
issues.quote: As an additional exploratory analysis, the results on the DRM procedure will be used as a possible predictor of the results on the MORI technique.

issues.description: The Extended Warning and Education about Memory conditions are delivered as purely auditory podcasts. The Demonstration and Motivation condition additionally involves an interactive memory task (writing down recalled DRM words), explicit individualized feedback from the experimenter, and a podcast. The conditions therefore differ not only in content but in modality, interactivity, personalization, and cognitive engagement. Any observed difference between Demonstration and Motivation and the other conditions could be due to these procedural confounds rather than the theoretical components of the intervention.
issues.quote: Participants in the 'Extended warning' group will listen to the podcast... those in the 'Education about memory' group will listen to the podcast... Participants in the DRM group will be given the DRM procedure with feedback... Afterwards, the participants will be motivated to resist illegitimate influences.

issues.subcategory: weakly justified rank-ordering of intervention efficacy
issues.description: The manuscript predicts a specific rank order of effectiveness: Demonstration and Motivation > Extended Warning > Education about Memory. This hierarchy is derived from a loose analogy to Sagarin et al.'s findings in a different domain (persuasion resistance) and the assumption that demonstrating effects is stronger than lecturing. However, no theoretical principle or empirical evidence directly supports this ordering in the memory conformity context. Extended Warning includes explicit enlightenment about the deception (which IMP theory specifically identifies as highly effective), and Education about Memory activates metamemory processes shown to reduce suggestibility. The predicted rank order appears post-hoc and may set up unfalsifiable interpretations.
issues.quote: we tentatively assume that the most effective technique in reducing the memory conformity effect will be Demonstration and motivation... Extended warning against misinformation is expected to be slightly less effective than Demonstration and motivation but more effective than Education about memory.

issues.subcategory: potential interference between DRM task and crime film memory
issues.description: In the Demonstration and Motivation condition, participants are exposed to DRM word lists (including lists related to medical and other semantic categories) and then immediately complete the individual memory test about the crime film. The DRM procedure involves deep semantic processing of category-related words that were not presented (false recall). This proactive semantic interference could impair memory retrieval from the film for this group specifically, independently of the intended motivational mechanism, creating a condition-specific source of noise or bias in the primary outcome measure.
issues.quote: First, in order to demonstrate to participants that they are vulnerable to influence, a substantially shortened and simplified procedure based on the DRM paradigm will be used... Immediately after the participants are done with the methods of reducing memory conformity (or the control condition), they will complete the individual memory test of the original material.

issues.subcategory: inconsistency in intervention timing rationale across manuscript sections
issues.description: In the main Introduction the authors write: 'In the present study we decided to place the warning after the collaborative recall (see the rationale for the research below).' In Section 1.1, they state the opposite: 'we decided to place the methods inducing resistance to misinformation before the collaborative recall phase.' The actual Procedure section then confirms the interventions are placed after collaborative recall. This three-way inconsistency suggests the rationale section was revised without updating earlier text, leaves the reader uncertain about the intended design rationale, and undermines the credibility of the theoretical justification.
issues.quote: In the present study we decided to place the warning after the collaborative recall... What is important, we decided to place the methods inducing resistance to misinformation before the collaborative recall phase

issues.description: The collaborative recall uses a PowerPoint presentation with five-choice options displayed for 60 seconds. This structured recognition format differs substantially from the free-recall discussion that occurs between real co-witnesses. Additionally, if pairs cannot agree, both responses are recorded, but the analysis plan provides no rule for how to handle such disagreement cases when classifying whether misinformation was delivered. Furthermore, the fact that responses are selected from a fixed set may constrain the co-witness influence process in ways that reduce external validity.
issues.quote: Each question and its five possible responses will be displayed in a PowerPoint presentation for 60 seconds while participants discuss the answer. If the participants are unable to reach an agreement, both responses will be documented.

issues.subcategory: inadequate reporting of effect size heterogeneity explanation
issues.description: The enormous discrepancy between the two baseline effect sizes (g = 1.92 vs. g = 0.38) is noted but unexplained. Given that these studies used virtually the same procedure with Polish samples, this variance is remarkable and warrants substantive investigation. Possible explanations (e.g., sample characteristics, specific counterbalancing versions used, differences in the collaborative recall procedure, demand characteristics, year of data collection) are not discussed. Simply applying a random-effects model to average over unexplained heterogeneity produces a point estimate that may not generalize, and proceeding without examining moderators weakens the evidential basis for the power analysis.
issues.quote: The existing results as regards effect sizes are Hedges' g = 1.92, N = 55 (Ito et al., 2019) and Hedges' g = 0.38, N = 74 (Kękuś et al., 2020). Given the rather large difference in effect sizes between both studies, random effects were assumed while calculating the joint effect size

issues.subcategory: typographical errors and inconsistent citation format
issues.description: There are several typographical errors and citation inconsistencies throughout the manuscript. 'Familarised' (Introduction) should be 'familiarised.' The reference to the Szpitalak et al. (2019) study is incomplete: the body reference reads 'Szpitalak et al (2019)' (missing period after 'al') and the full citation in the references gives the journal page range as '1–10,' which is atypical. In-text citations inconsistently use 'and' vs. '&' (e.g., 'Oeberst and Blank, 2012' vs. '(Blank & Launay, 2014)'). A bullet point in section 1.1.2 is not preceded by a dash unlike the others. These errors suggest incomplete copyediting.
issues.quote: participants first are familarised with some original material... Szpitalak et al (2019)... Oeberst and Blank, 2012

issues.subcategory: missing analysis plan for certainty ratings
issues.description: The Procedure section specifies that participants will rate their subjective certainty for each answer on a 0–100% scale, which is a potentially informative measure of calibration, confidence-accuracy relationships, and metacognitive monitoring. However, the Analysis Plan makes no mention of how these certainty ratings will be analyzed, what hypotheses they are intended to address, or whether they are primary or secondary outcomes. Given the central role of confidence in theories of the misinformation effect (including the IMP framework invoked here), this omission represents an important analytic gap.
issues.quote: for each question, the participants will be asked to rate the subjective certainty of each answer on a scale from 0% (complete uncertainty, guessing) to 100% (absolute certainty).
